A 29-year-old woman visits her primary care provider due to intermittent episodes of bright pink urine
over the past few days, which she fears may be blood. Her medical history is unremarkable, and she
denies recent illness. She has only taken a few ibuprofen tablets for menstrual cramps and does not
consume alcohol or smoke. Vital signs include a temperature of 36.5°C (97.7°F), pulse of 77/min,
respiratory rate of 16/min, and blood pressure of 149/95 mm Hg. Physical examination reveals 2+
pitting edema extending to her knees. Urinalysis shows RBCs, RBC casts, and acanthocytes without
proteinuria. Laboratory results include a serum creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen of 42
mg/dL, serum potassium of 4.8 mEq/L, serum sodium of 140 mEq/L, and serum chloride of 102 mEq/L.
What is the most appropriate next step in managing this patient? Answer Choices: (A) 24-hour urine
protein collection (B) Empiric corticosteroid therapy (C) ANCA serologies (D) Non-contrast computed
tomography (CT) (E) Discontinuation of NSAID (F) Initiation of antihypertensive therapy (G) Renal
ultrasound with Doppler (H) Intravenous (IV) fluid therapy and electrolyte correction (I) Renal biopsy (J)
Complement level testing (C3, C4)
 A. ANCA serologies
B. Renal ultrasound with Doppler
C. Complement level testing (C3, C4)
D. Discontinuation of NSAID
E. Empiric corticosteroid therapy
F. Non-contrast computed tomography (CT)
G. Initiation of antihypertensive therapy
H. Intravenous (IV) fluid therapy and electrolyte correction
I. 24-hour urine protein collection
J. Renal biopsy
